stories.head: Ukraine and Russia say emergency alert apps were hacked
stories.say: Ukraine's nationwide air raid app sent false warnings of nuclear and chemical threats in Kyiv on Sunday, and Russia says its own emergencies app was also hit by a cyberattack.
stories.stand: Ukraine's air raid app sent false nuclear and chemical warnings for Kyiv on Sunday, and Russia said its own emergencies app was attacked.
body: Ukraine's nationwide air raid alert app sent false warnings on Sunday, telling users that Kyiv and other areas faced nuclear, chemical and street combat threats. One message said Russia had deployed its Oreshnik hypersonic missile.

Ukraine's Air Force said on Telegram that the app appeared to have been subjected to enemy influence, and that there was no radiation threat. Ukraine's Centre for Strategic Communications blamed Russia. No group claimed responsibility.
Early on Monday, Russia's Emergencies Ministry said its own mobile app had suffered a massive cyberattack that spread false information. It was not clear whether the two incidents were linked.

The incidents came after a six-day localised truce around Oleshky in the Kherson region ended on Sunday. Ukraine's digital transformation ministry said its app was not operating, but sirens still worked.

stories.head: Longest local truce of Ukraine war ends in Kherson region
stories.say: A six-day ceasefire around the Russian-held town of Oleshky, mediated by Melania Trump, expired on Sunday night after allowing civilians to be evacuated.
stories.stand: A six-day ceasefire around Russian-held Oleshky, mediated by Melania Trump, expired on Sunday without an extension after civilian evacuations.
body: A six-day local ceasefire covering the Russian-held town of Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from Kherson, expired on Sunday night. It was the longest local pause in fighting since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

The truce was mediated by US First Lady Melania Trump, with Pope Leo XIV involved. Officials on both sides said it held from Tuesday without violations, allowing evacuations, de-mining and deliveries of food and medicine.
A Ukrainian official told AFP that Russia had refused a Kyiv proposal to extend it. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow viewed the operation positively.

Ukraine's military said 167 more civilians, including 22 children, were evacuated from threatened areas on Sunday. Kherson governor Oleksandr Prokudin urged residents to avoid red zones near the river. Elsewhere, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian attacks on energy sites in four regions cut power to hundreds of thousands of households.

stories.head: Nine killed as business jet crashes near homes in Florida
stories.say: A business jet flying from Texas to the Bahamas crashed near homes in Palm Beach County on Sunday, killing all nine people on board; no one on the ground was hurt.
stories.stand: A Learjet 60 flying from Austin to the Bahamas crashed in Palm Beach County on Sunday, killing everyone on board.
body: A Learjet 60 business jet crashed near homes in Palm Beach County, Florida, on Sunday afternoon, killing all nine people on board. It had left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas for the Bahamas, the FAA said.
Governor Ron DeSantis said no one on the ground was hurt. About 600 people were evacuated from the area, according to CBS News.

Air traffic control audio captured the pilot declaring an emergency and reporting a rapid, overspeed descent before saying the plane was going to crash. The pilot had earlier reported ice and turbulence, the Jerusalem Post reported, citing CNN.
The National Transportation Safety Board has sent a team to investigate. No cause has been given, and the victims have not been named.

stories.head: UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years
stories.say: The UN's peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has begun shutting down after Russia vetoed its renewal, and Antonio Guterres has urged all sides to show maximum restraint.
stories.stand: MINURSO began winding down on Sunday after Russia vetoed a US draft to renew it, and the UN chief urged maximum restraint.
body: The UN mission in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO, has ended after 35 years, Secretary-General Antonio Guterres confirmed on Sunday. A liquidation phase began on 1 November, with assets being returned to troop-contributing countries.

The Security Council failed to renew its mandate on Friday. Russia vetoed a US draft that had 11 of 15 votes and would have made Morocco's autonomy plan the only basis for talks. A rival Russian text was rejected.

Guterres said he was concerned about the risk of hostilities escalating and urged all parties to show maximum restraint. The mission was set up in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire and organise a referendum, which never took place.

Morocco's royal palace called the outcome a significant development. Algeria expressed deep regret and accused the US of bias towards Morocco. The Polisario Front said it was concerned by the deadlock.

stories.head: France opens attempted murder inquiry after petrol bomb thrown at police
stories.say: French prosecutors have opened an attempted murder inquiry after a petrol bomb was thrown at police during Saturday's cost-of-living protests across France.
stories.stand: Paris prosecutors are investigating an attack on police during Saturday's protests, as about 320,000 people marched across France.
body: Paris prosecutors have opened an attempted murder investigation after a petrol bomb was thrown at police during cost-of-living protests on Saturday. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez described the attack as attempted murder.
Prosecutors said objects were thrown at about 15 police officers and gendarmes. Some suffered second-degree burns, and no suspects had been detained, according to El Tiempo.

The interior ministry put nationwide turnout at about 320,000, including 70,000 in Paris. Most marches were peaceful, but there were clashes in Marseille, Lyon and Toulouse, and hundreds of people were detained.
The movement grew out of anger over learning conditions and living costs, and has widened to civil liberties. Student groups plan further school blockades.

stories.head: Shops looted as German youth protests turn violent
stories.say: Youth-led protests over the cost of living turned violent in several German cities late on Saturday, with shops looted in Frankfurt and water cannon used in Hamburg and Cologne.
stories.stand: Mostly peaceful protests by the youth group Gen Z regelt ended in looting and clashes with police in Frankfurt, Hamburg and Cologne.
body: Youth-led protests over the cost of living turned violent in several German cities late on Saturday. In Frankfurt, masked rioters smashed shop windows and looted goods, police said.
Frankfurt police said protesters threw stones, fireworks and pepper bombs, and some threw Molotov cocktails at officers. Weapons stolen from a gun shop were later recovered.
In Hamburg, police used water cannon and tear gas against protesters who burned barricades. Police also used water cannon in Cologne, and there were clashes in Berlin.

The protests, organised by a group called Gen Z regelt, took place in more than 30 cities. Demonstrators called for better education, health care and affordable living, and opposed a return of conscription. Most were peaceful until the evening.

stories.head: UN demands inquiry after staff member dies in Houthi custody
stories.say: The UN has demanded an independent investigation after a Yemeni member of its human rights staff died in Houthi custody, having been held since June 2024.
stories.stand: A Yemeni employee of the UN Human Rights Office, detained by the Houthis since June 2024, has died, the UN said.
body: A Yemeni staff member of the UN Human Rights Office has died in the custody of Yemen's Houthis, the UN said. He had been held since 6 June 2024.

UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the family learned of the death more than a month after it happened and had been given no explanation. He demanded medical and detention records and an urgent, independent investigation.
Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was appalled. He noted it was the second death of a UN employee in Houthi detention, after a World Food Programme worker died in 2025.

Seven colleagues from Türk's office remain detained. Yemen's Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani said more than 70 UN staff are held and that the Houthis bear full responsibility. No Houthi response was reported.

stories.head: Swiss foreign minister visits North Korea for first time since 2003
stories.say: Ignazio Cassis has become the first Swiss foreign minister to visit North Korea since 2003, meeting Choe Son Hui as Switzerland reopened its office in Pyongyang.
stories.stand: Ignazio Cassis met North Korea's foreign minister in Pyongyang as Switzerland formally reopened its diplomatic office there.
body: Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis has visited Pyongyang, the first trip by a Swiss foreign minister to North Korea since 2003. He was there on 29 and 30 October for the formal reopening of Switzerland's office.

Cassis met Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui. He said on X they discussed regularising political relations, re-establishing dialogue and security on the Korean Peninsula. North Korea's state media said talks were friendly, Euronews reported.
The office has operated since 19 October and reports to the Swiss embassy in Beijing. A previous office closed in 2020 during the pandemic.
Cassis then went to Seoul to meet South Korean officials. South Korea's military said North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles on Thursday.

stories.head: Indian opposition rallies in Delhi to demand election chief's removal
stories.say: Opposition leaders led by Rahul Gandhi rallied in New Delhi on Sunday, demanding the removal of India's chief election commissioner over a revision of voter rolls.
stories.stand: Opposition leaders including Rahul Gandhi addressed a packed rally on Sunday over the revision of India's voter rolls.
body: India's opposition INDIA bloc held a rally at Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi on Sunday. Thousands attended to demand the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, according to The Wire.

The protest targets the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. Opposition parties accuse the commission of removing eligible voters to help Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party. The commission and government have denied wrongdoing.

Rahul Gandhi, the Leader of the Opposition, claimed 13.3 crore voters had been removed from the rolls. He promised legal action against Kumar, Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah. Other speakers included Mallikarjun Kharge, Akhilesh Yadav and Mamata Banerjee.
The Bharatiya Janata Party held a separate march on the same day, marking the anniversary of the 1984 anti-Sikh riots. The Aam Aadmi Party and the DMK stayed away from the rally.

stories.head: Israeli strikes kill eight in Gaza, medics say
stories.say: Israeli strikes killed eight people in Gaza on Sunday, medics said, five in Khan Younis and three in Gaza City; Israel's military said it struck militants in Khan Younis.
stories.stand: Strikes hit Khan Younis and Gaza City on Sunday, as Israel and Hamas trade accusations over a year-old ceasefire.
body: Israeli strikes killed eight people in the Gaza Strip on Sunday, according to medics and Gaza's civil defence. Five were killed in Khan Younis and three in Gaza City.

Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said the five killed in western Khan Younis were police officers. Israel's military said it struck several militants in Khan Younis. It did not comment on the Gaza City strike.

Israel says Hamas has been rearming in breach of a year-old US-brokered ceasefire, which Hamas denies. Gaza health officials say at least 1,500 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the truce.

stories.head: Iliana Iotova wins Bulgarian presidency, first woman elected to the post
stories.say: Acting President Iliana Iotova, who favours dialogue with Moscow, has won Bulgaria's presidential run-off, becoming the first woman elected head of state.
stories.stand: The acting president, who favours dialogue with Moscow, beat pro-Western candidate Andrey Gyurov in Sunday's run-off, preliminary results show.
body: Acting President Iliana Iotova has won Bulgaria's presidential run-off, according to preliminary official results. With 99.68% of protocols counted, she had 57.66% against 39.38% for Andrey Gyurov, Infobae reported.
She becomes the first woman elected head of state in Bulgaria. The presidency is largely ceremonial.

Iotova advocates dialogue with Moscow and opposes military aid to Ukraine. Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister, was backed by the pro-Western opposition and favoured support for Kyiv.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated her and called for a strong Bulgaria in a strong Europe. Exit polls put turnout at about 27% to 29%.

stories.head: Trump says Flavio Bolsonaro can stay in US as long as he wants
stories.say: Donald Trump says Flavio Bolsonaro, who left Brazil after losing the presidential run-off, can stay in the US as long as he wants; Marco Rubio denied any US role in his flight.
stories.stand: The defeated Brazilian candidate left Brazil despite a passport order, and Marco Rubio denied the US helped him leave.
body: Donald Trump said on Saturday that Flavio Bolsonaro can stay in the United States as long as he wants. Speaking at Mar-a-Lago, he said Bolsonaro had been treated very shabbily and called Brazil's election a disgrace.

Bolsonaro lost the 25 October run-off to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and has not conceded. He arrived near Miami on 28 October after leaving Brazil via Argentina, despite an order to give up his passport.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US government did not facilitate his departure. Bolsonaro is under investigation in Brazil over alleged money laundering, which he calls persecution. Reuters reported he was admitted under humanitarian parole.
Brazil summoned an Argentine diplomat over the episode. Reports say Jason Miller helped arrange the journey, which the US has not confirmed.

stories.head: Henry Nowak's family describe pain of watching police footage
stories.say: Henry Nowak's family say watching police footage of the dying student being handcuffed changed their world a second time, after his killing in Southampton.
stories.stand: The family of the 18-year-old stabbed in Southampton speak for the first time ahead of an ITV documentary.
body: The family of Henry Nowak, an 18-year-old student stabbed in Southampton on 3 December 2025, have described the pain of watching police footage of his final moments. They spoke for the first time to ITV News editor Paul Brand for a documentary.

Body-worn camera video shows officers handcuffing Henry after his killer falsely accused him of racial abuse. He repeatedly told them he had been stabbed. His stepmother Katie said the family's world had changed twice: when they learned of his death and when they saw the video.

Vickrum Digwa, 23, was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years. His mother, Kiran Kaur, was jailed for assisting an offender after removing the knife. The Meon Valley Times reports that the police watchdog is investigating 2 officers for potential gross misconduct.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has ordered an independent review led by former lord chancellor Alex Chalk. The documentary, Dear Henry: Our Fight For Justice, airs on ITV on Thursday 5 November at 9pm.

stories.head: Five teenage boys stabbed at Halloween party in Hampshire
stories.say: Five teenage boys were seriously hurt when, police believe, an unknown group got into a Halloween party in Chandler's Ford in Hampshire on Saturday night.
stories.stand: Three 16-year-olds and two 17-year-olds were taken to hospital; no arrests have been reported.
body: Five teenage boys were seriously injured in a stabbing at a Halloween party in Chandler's Ford, Hampshire, on Saturday night. Police were called to the house on Park Road shortly after 10.30pm.
Three of the boys are 16 and two are 17. All were taken to hospital with serious injuries. Detectives believe an unknown group got into the party.

No arrests have been reported. Detective Chief Inspector Elizabeth Pirie said officers were working to identify everyone who was at the party. Park Road and Valley Road were cordoned off overnight, and police have appealed for CCTV, dashcam and phone footage.

stories.head: More than 300 arrested at Palestine Action protest at US embassy
stories.say: Police in London said 325 people were arrested at a protest backing Palestine Action outside the US embassy on Saturday, days before a Supreme Court challenge to the ban.
stories.stand: Most were held under the Terrorism Act for showing support for the proscribed group, ahead of a Supreme Court appeal.
body: The Metropolitan Police said 325 people were arrested at a protest supporting Palestine Action outside the US embassy in Nine Elms, south-west London, on Saturday. Of those, 320 were held for expressing support for a proscribed organisation under the Terrorism Act.

The protest was organised by the campaign group Defend Our Juries. Officers began making arrests shortly after 12.30pm under a dispersal order covering the embassy grounds. Police Scotland said no arrests were made at a separate protest outside the US consulate in Edinburgh.
Defend Our Juries said Margaret Owen, a 94-year-old human rights lawyer, was among those arrested. The group says more than 4,000 people have now been detained for defying the ban since July 2025.
The protest came ahead of a Supreme Court appeal against the group's proscription, due to begin on 4 November. The Court of Appeal ruled in June that the ban was lawful.

stories.head: Drones halt flights at Jersey Airport for a second night
stories.say: Drone activity near Jersey Airport stopped flights landing for a second night on Saturday, with services from Heathrow, Gatwick and Southampton cancelled.
stories.stand: Police are appealing for help to find the operators as the island's government seeks counter-drone support from UK agencies.
body: Drones near Jersey Airport stopped flights from landing for a second night on Saturday. Airport staff reported drone activity near the airfield shortly after 8pm.
Services from Heathrow, Gatwick and Southampton were cancelled. On Friday evening, 3 flights were diverted back to the UK after drones entered the airport's restricted airspace.

Police inspector Rob McCallum said two or three drones had entered restricted airspace, according to Gulf News. States of Jersey Police have asked islanders to call 999 if they see anyone flying a drone, and not to approach them.
Chief Minister Lyndon Farnham said the government was working with UK agencies on detection and counter-drone technology.

stories.head: Part of Pero's Bridge collapses into Bristol harbour
stories.say: Part of Bristol's Pero's Bridge, closed since it failed during testing in the summer, collapsed into the harbour late on Saturday. The council says no one was hurt.
stories.stand: No one was injured but hydraulic oil leaked into the water from the closed lifting footbridge.
body: Part of Pero's Bridge, a lifting footbridge in Bristol's harbour, collapsed into the water shortly before 11pm on Saturday. No one was injured, according to Bristol City Council.
Andrew Brown, who chairs the council's harbour committee, said the central span slipped. A small amount of hydraulic oil leaked into the water, and environmental specialists were sent to clear it.

The bridge, designed by Eilis O'Connell and opened in 1999, has been closed since it malfunctioned during testing in the summer. The council has set aside about £1.5 million for repairs and says the refurbishment plans are not yet affected.

stories.head: Fireworks aimed at fire crews in Northern Ireland on Halloween
stories.say: Fireworks were deliberately aimed at firefighters at six call-outs in Northern Ireland on Halloween night, during a busy shift that included twenty-three bonfires.
stories.stand: The fire service attended 89 incidents overnight and said no one was hurt in the attacks.
body: Fireworks were deliberately aimed at firefighters at 6 incidents in Northern Ireland on Halloween night, the Northern Ireland Fire and Rescue Service said.
The service responded to 89 incidents between 6pm on Saturday and 1am on Sunday. Several were linked to Halloween, including 23 bonfires.
A spokesperson said no damage or injuries resulted and the service kept up its response to local communities throughout.

stories.head: Home Office launches knife crime campaign in London hotspots
stories.say: A Home Office campaign called No Place for Knives launched on Monday in parts of Westminster and Croydon, warning offenders of more patrols and facial recognition.
stories.stand: Adverts in Westminster, Croydon and Birmingham warn of more patrols, metal detection and live facial recognition.
body: The Home Office launched a knife crime campaign, No Place for Knives, in parts of Westminster and Croydon on Monday. Adverts at tube stations, bus stops and on social media warn offenders of more police activity.
The messages highlight smarter metal detection, rapid response e-bikes, extra foot patrols and live facial recognition. The campaign is also being piloted in Birmingham city centre.

More than £8.1 million from the Knife Crime Concentrations Fund is going to Westminster, Croydon and 16 other London boroughs. The government says knife crime in London has fallen 14% since the general election.
Policing minister Sarah Jones and Metropolitan Police Commander Pete Stevens backed the campaign.

stories.head: Five British anti-migrant activists expelled from France
stories.say: Five British men accused by French authorities of belonging to an ultra-right movement have been expelled after police found tear gas canisters in their minibus near Dunkirk.
stories.stand: French police arrested the men near Dunkirk, where officials say they livestreamed intimidation of migrants from a minibus.
body: Five British men described by French authorities as members of an ultra-right movement have been expelled from France. They were arrested on Thursday in Grande-Synthe, near Dunkirk.

The men, aged 30 to 46, travelled the northern French coast in a minibus they called the Battle Bus. Officials said they livestreamed acts of intimidation against migrants trying to reach the UK. Police said they found 4 tear gas canisters.

They were held on suspicion of joining a group formed to prepare violence and carrying weapons without legitimate reason. London999 reported that Dunkirk prosecutor Charlotte Huet said investigators had not established evidence of violent offences.
Each man was reportedly fined about £2,500 and banned from the Nord and Pas-de-Calais departments for 6 months.

stories.head: Channel crossings resume with 934 arrivals in two days
stories.say: Nine hundred and thirty-four people crossed the Channel in small boats on Thursday and Friday, ending a three-week pause in arrivals caused by bad weather.
stories.stand: Arrivals restarted after 21 days without crossings, taking the 2026 total to 21,869, Home Office figures show.
body: A total of 934 people crossed the Channel in small boats on Thursday and Friday, ending a 21-day pause caused by bad weather. Home Office figures show 263 people arrived in 3 boats on Thursday and 671 in 9 boats on Friday.
The pause was the longest without arrivals this year. Arrivals for 2026 reached 21,869 after Friday, according to Home Office figures reported by LBC.

ITV reported that the total before Friday was 43% lower than at the same point in 2025. The government says this summer's arrivals were the lowest since 2020. Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said Labour was too weak to stop the boats.

stories.say: A thirty-five-year-old man has been charged with possessing explosives after a security alert in the Shankill area of north Belfast that forced residents from their homes.
stories.stand: Homes in north Belfast were evacuated during searches by terrorism detectives that uncovered several suspicious devices.
body: A 35-year-old man has been charged with possessing explosives after a security alert in the Shankill area of north Belfast. Police said he faces 2 counts of possessing explosives under suspicious circumstances, plus possessing a prohibited weapon.

Detectives from the PSNI's Terrorism Investigation Unit searched properties in Edwina Street on Friday, the Irish News reported. Police said several suspicious devices were found. DUP MLA Brian Kingston said about 40 houses were evacuated.
The man is due before Belfast Magistrates' Court on Monday. Detective Chief Inspector McCallum said all cordons had been lifted and residents had been allowed home.

stories.head: Build-to-rent starts fall by more than 63%, industry figures show
stories.say: Construction starts on build-to-rent homes have fallen by more than sixty-three per cent in a year, an industry group says, blaming rising costs and planning delays.
stories.stand: Industry group Real Estate:UK says rising costs and planning delays have pushed rental development to breaking point.
body: Construction starts on build-to-rent homes fell by more than 63% in the year to the third quarter of 2026, according to industry group Real Estate:UK. Annual starts dropped from 12,674 to 4,696, Letting Agent Today reported.
Completions reached 21,979, exceeding starts for the 11th quarter in a row. Homes under construction fell 30% nationally over the 12 months to September, and new starts outside London fell 78%.

The group blamed rising building and financing costs, planning delays, taxes and delays at the Building Safety Regulator. Director Danny Pinder said the viability crisis was pushing development of rental homes to breaking point.

stories.head: Rail security campaign marks ten years with 83,000 crimes recorded
stories.say: The See it. Say it. Sorted. rail campaign has reached ten years, with the government saying almost eighty-three thousand crimes were recorded through its text number.
stories.stand: The government says reports to British Transport Police's text number have led to more than 175,000 deployments since 2016.
body: The rail security campaign See it. Say it. Sorted. has marked its 10th anniversary, the Department for Transport and the British Transport Police Authority said on Saturday. It was launched in 2016.

Almost 83,000 crimes have been recorded through the 61016 text number, from more than 1.5 million texts to British Transport Police. The reports led to more than 175,000 police deployments, according to the government.

The government also pointed to £63 million over 3 years for British Transport Police, funding more than 200 extra officers. Rail minister Lord Hendy and Chief Constable Lucy D'Orsi marked the milestone.

stories.head: Michigan Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Republican Mike Rogers for Senate
stories.say: Haley Stevens, who lost Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, has endorsed Republican Mike Rogers, and the state party chair says she is no longer a member.
stories.stand: Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to Abdul El-Sayed, backed his Republican rival two days before the election.
body: Democratic Representative Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's Senate race on Sunday, according to The Jerusalem Post and VIN News. She announced it in a video and appeared with Rogers at Perfecting Church in Detroit.

Stevens narrowly lost the August Democratic primary to Abdul El-Sayed. She had pressed him to condemn an outside group's ad linking US aid to Israel with grocery prices, which she called antisemitic. El-Sayed said his campaign did not make the ad and that he disagreed with it.

Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel said Stevens is not a current member of the party, VIN News reported. The Jerusalem Post said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the endorsement a despicable betrayal and that many of her staff resigned.
El-Sayed's campaign had earlier asked Stevens to stay away from its remaining events, CBS News reported. Her fiancé, Jason Turkish, has said he will vote for Rogers.

stories.head: Senator Chris Murphy in hospital after suffering a stroke
stories.say: Connecticut senator Chris Murphy is in hospital after a stroke on Saturday; his office says he is awake and alert and expected to make a full recovery.
stories.stand: The Connecticut Democrat, 53, is awake and alert at Johns Hopkins, and his office expects a full recovery.
body: Connecticut Democratic Senator Chris Murphy was taken to hospital on Saturday after a stroke, his office said. Chief of staff Allison Herwitt said he began feeling numbness in his arm at his son's hockey game.

He was first taken to a local hospital, then moved to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring. His office says he is awake and alert, is responding well to treatment and is expected to make a full recovery.
Murphy, 53, has served in the Senate since 2013. He is not on the ballot this year but had been campaigning for Democrats, and Fox News said he was due in New Hampshire on Sunday.

stories.head: Judge throws out Justice Department bid to delay Alaska Senate result
stories.say: A federal judge has thrown out a Justice Department lawsuit that sought to delay certifying Alaska's Senate race if Republican Dan Sullivan narrowly loses.
stories.stand: Judge Sharon Gleason said voters' choices could not be traced; Fox News reports the department will appeal.
body: A federal judge in Alaska dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit on Sunday that sought to delay certification of the state's Senate race. US District Judge Sharon Gleason ruled two days before Tuesday's vote.

The suit, filed on 22 October, targeted the possibility that Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses narrowly. It centred on a second candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., whom the department accuses of entering the race to confuse voters.

Gleason called the relief sought infeasible, Roll Call reported, saying ballots had been commingled and voters' choices could not be traced. Fox News said the department will appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

Democrat Mary Peltola denies involvement in recruiting the second candidate. The New York Times has reported that people linked to her campaign helped recruit him. Dan Sullivan says he will accept the result.

stories.head: Trump holds final midterm rallies in Iowa and Kansas
stories.say: Donald Trump closed his midterm campaign with rallies in Dubuque, Iowa, and Salina, Kansas, on Sunday, as Republicans defend their Senate majority.
stories.stand: The president campaigned in Dubuque and Salina on Sunday as Republicans defend Senate seats in two traditionally Republican states.
body: Donald Trump held a rally in Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday before heading to Salina, Kansas, in his final campaign push before Tuesday's midterms. The events had been cancelled and then reinstated, according to Al Jazeera and CBS News.

At the Five Flags Event Center, Trump spoke for about two hours, The Gazette reported. Senate nominee Ashley Hinson and governor nominee Zach Lahn joined him on stage, and a protester interrupted his remarks.

Republicans are defending a Senate seat and the governorship in Iowa, which Trump won by double digits in 2024. In Kansas, which last elected a Democratic senator in 1932, Senator Roger Marshall faces Democrat Adam Hamilton, a pastor.
Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority. Losing either chamber would let Democrats block Trump's agenda in his last two years, Al Jazeera noted.

stories.head: Control of Congress at stake as Americans vote on Tuesday
stories.say: Americans vote on Tuesday with control of Congress at stake; Republicans defend a fifty-three to forty-seven Senate majority, and over fifty-two million have already voted.
stories.stand: Republicans defend narrow majorities in both chambers, with all 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats and 36 governorships on the ballot.
body: Americans vote on Tuesday 3 November in midterm elections that will decide control of Congress. Republicans hold the Senate 53-47 and a narrow majority in the House, Fox News and Al Jazeera report.
All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot, according to Al Jazeera. Fox News says governorships are being contested in 36 of 50 states, along with 145 statewide ballot measures.

More than 52 million people had already voted, a midterm record, Al Jazeera reported, citing the University of Florida's Election Lab. CBS News, citing the same source, put the figure at about 49.6 million as of Friday evening.
Fox News rates Senate control a toss-up. CBS News lists Maine, Michigan, Ohio, Texas and Alaska among its Senate toss-ups. The first polls close at 6pm ET in parts of Kentucky and Indiana.

stories.head: Rachel Reeves says Britain's future lies inside the EU
stories.say: Former chancellor Rachel Reeves says Britain's future lies in the European Union, arguing that Brexit has made the country poorer, weaker and less secure.
stories.stand: In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury, the former chancellor said Brexit had left Britain poorer, weaker and less secure.
body: Former chancellor Rachel Reeves has argued that Britain's future lies in the European Union, City AM reported on Sunday. In a Sunday Times article, her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury, she said Brexit had made the country poorer, weaker and less secure.

Reeves helped write Labour's 2024 manifesto, which ruled out rejoining the EU. She said supporters of re-entry must show tangible benefits, and called for progress on a youth mobility scheme before a UK-EU summit later this month.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has named full membership, the single market and the customs union as possible options. He says any change would need a mandate at a general election, due by 2029. The Conservatives oppose reopening the Brexit debate, and Reform says there is no mandate.

body: Chancellor John Healey said on Sunday that Labour will reduce the benefits bill, with changes starting next year. Speaking on the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg programme, he said the system was not working and needed big changes, City AM reported.
Healey had earlier declined to give a timeframe for cutting welfare costs before the next election. He said the rate of increase had slowed since Labour took office.

The Office for Budget Responsibility puts public debt at about 95% of GDP. It says Healey needs an extra £11bn to stop day-to-day spending falling 2.6% in real terms late in its forecast. Former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane called the Budget small beer.

stories.stand: Emma Reynolds defended Budget tax rises as targeted and fair, as business owners argued Labour had broken its manifesto pledge.
body: Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said on GB News that employers are not working people but companies, City AM reported on Sunday. Her comments addressed claims that Labour broke its manifesto pledge.

Labour's 2024 manifesto promised not to raise taxes on working people, ruling out rises in income tax, employee National Insurance and VAT. Critics say changes to employer taxes and frozen thresholds broke that promise.

Reynolds said the tax rises in Chancellor John Healey's first Budget were targeted and fair. Business groups criticised the cut in Business Asset Disposal Relief from £1m to £500,000 and higher taxes on savings and rental income from April 2027.

stories.stand: The Conservative leader says unfunded promises will require substantial tax rises; the report carried no government response.
body: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Chancellor John Healey of leaving a £49bn black hole in the public finances, City AM reported on Sunday. She said it would require substantial tax rises.

Badenoch said taxes would need to rise by about £1,700 per household a year by 2030/31 to pay for unfunded promises. Writing in The Telegraph, she put the shortfall in meeting a defence target of 3% of GDP at £11bn in 2030/31.

She also pointed to a National Care Service pledged by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, which economists expect could cost up to £18bn a year. City AM said Burnham plans to switch the pension triple lock to a double lock from 2030 to help pay for it. The report included no government response.

stories.say: Andy Burnham is open to talks on a state apology for the slave trade but has ruled out reparations, offering debt relief instead ahead of the Commonwealth summit in Antigua.
stories.stand: Ahead of the Commonwealth summit in Antigua, the prime minister proposed dialogue on a state apology and debt relief instead of payments.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has proposed a structured dialogue on a formal British state apology for the transatlantic slave trade, but has ruled out financial reparations, IBTimes UK reported. He set out his position in a Guardian article on 30 October.

Instead, Burnham proposed easing debt pressures on vulnerable countries through longer repayment periods and better interest rates. Antigua and Barbuda's prime minister, Gaston Browne, welcomed the debt offer but maintained the Caribbean's call for reparatory justice.

The Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting runs from 1 to 4 November in St John's, Antigua. King Charles III opens it on Tuesday 3 November. Buckingham Palace says he will not offer a formal apology or commit to reparations.

stories.head: South Africa's parties make final pitches before local elections
stories.say: South Africans choose local councils on Wednesday, with polls pointing to coalitions in most big cities, as Cyril Ramaphosa admits the ANC has had shortcomings.
stories.stand: Polls suggest coalitions are likely in most big cities as voters choose councils across all nine provinces on Wednesday.
body: South Africans vote on Wednesday 4 November for councils across all nine provinces, Daily Maverick reports. Polls suggest coalitions are likely in most major metros.

At a rally in Mdantsane on Sunday, President Cyril Ramaphosa admitted the ANC had shortcomings. DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis told supporters in Mamelodi on Saturday that the contest was a two-horse race between the ANC and DA.

Jacob Zuma, in his first public appearance since being hospitalised, told an MK party rally in Durban it would fight until the unity government ends. EFF leader Julius Malema focused on failing services at a rally in Soweto.
An eNCA/Mark Data poll in Johannesburg put the DA on 35% and the ANC on 21.8%. An eNCA/Mark Data poll predicts turnout of 48.8%, down from 58.6% in 2024.

stories.head: National Grid buys Teesside land for UK's biggest substation
stories.say: National Grid has agreed to buy more than seventy acres on Teesside for what would be Britain's biggest substation, close to a planned data centre site.
stories.stand: The grid operator has agreed a land deal at Teesworks for a substation that could serve a planned data centre with up to 3.2GW.
body: National Grid has agreed to buy more than 70 acres of land at Dorman Point on the Teesworks site in Teesside. The deal was signed in the week before it was reported on Sunday 1 November.

The land would host what reports describe as Britain's biggest electricity substation. It would serve a planned data centre nearby. Tees Valley mayor Ben Houchen said up to 3.2GW of capacity would let the area compete for such projects.

Balfour Beatty is reportedly in line to deliver the substation. Steel River Power, which runs the estate's private electricity network, is also involved. National Grid's Matt Pearce said the company would work with partners to move quickly. No financial terms were disclosed.

stories.head: India's GST collections jump 22.9% in October
stories.say: India's gross goods and services tax collections rose almost twenty-three per cent in October, to two point three one lakh crore rupees, led by tax on imports.
stories.stand: Gross goods and services tax revenue reached ₹2.31 lakh crore, with tax on imports rising much faster than domestic revenue.
body: India's gross goods and services tax (GST) collections rose 22.9% year on year to ₹2.31 lakh crore in October, according to provisional government data released on Sunday 1 November.
Imports drove the rise, with revenue up 42.2% to ₹72,246 crore. Domestic revenue grew more slowly, by 15.8% to about ₹1.59 lakh crore.
Refunds rose 6.5% to ₹27,934 crore, so net collections climbed 25.6% to about ₹2.03 lakh crore. Gross collections for April to October were up 13.2% on a year earlier.

stories.head: Tesco sells Czech and Slovak stores for about £1.5bn
stories.say: Tesco is selling its Czech and Slovak businesses to Ahold Delhaize for about one and a half billion pounds, and says it will review all options for Hungary.
stories.stand: The UK's biggest grocer is selling the two businesses to Ahold Delhaize, leaving Hungary under review as its global retreat continues.
body: Tesco has agreed to sell its businesses in the Czech Republic and Slovakia to Ahold Delhaize for about £1.5bn. Chief executive Ken Murphy announced the deal on Friday 30 October.
The two businesses had combined sales of £2.9bn last year. They made up most of the profit of Tesco's central European arm. The sale is expected to complete in 2027.
Hungary is not part of the deal, and Tesco says it will review all options there. City AM reports that a tax on foreign-owned retailers and a cap on grocery markups may be deterring buyers.
Ken Murphy said the sale would simplify the group and focus it on its UK and Irish businesses.

stories.say: IDBI Bank staff in India have called a two-day strike against the sale of a controlling stake in the lender to Canada's Fairfax Financial Holdings for 5.5 billion dollars.
stories.stand: Unions and opposition leader Rahul Gandhi oppose the government's sale of a controlling stake in IDBI Bank to Fairfax Financial Holdings.
body: Employees of India's IDBI Bank have called a two-day nationwide strike against its sale to Canada's Fairfax Financial Holdings. The United Forum of IDBI Officers and Employees announced the action on Sunday 1 November.

The government approved the sale of a 60.72% stake on 14 October for about $5.5bn. Fairfax is paying 81 rupees a share, above a fair value of 75.99 rupees. The government and LIC are selling their holdings.

Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi backed the unions, saying public banks are tools to build the nation. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the bank was revived with more than 250 billion rupees of recapitalisation. The deal needs Reserve Bank of India approval.

stories.stand: Canada's prime minister reported a good call with Donald Trump, months after talks collapsed and the US imposed 50% tariffs.
body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Sunday that he had a "good conversation" with US President Donald Trump about trade. His office said the call took place on Saturday.
Mr Carney said teams from both countries would work in the coming weeks to deliver a deal. He said it would build on recent constructive discussions.

High-level talks broke down in August. The US then imposed 50% tariffs on Canadian goods. Al Jazeera says the levy covers $20bn of goods, about 5.5% of Canada's exports, and that Canada retaliated with its own tariffs.
The call came two days before the US midterm elections. Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre urged Mr Carney to get a great deal.

stories.head: Bank of England expected to raise rates for first time since 2023
stories.say: Economists expect the Bank of England to raise interest rates on Thursday for the first time since August 2023, as higher energy prices push up inflation.
stories.stand: Economists polled by Reuters expect Bank Rate to rise from 3.75% to 4.0% on Thursday as energy costs push inflation higher.
body: The Bank of England is expected to raise Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4.0% on Thursday, according to a Reuters poll of economists. It would be the first increase since August 2023.

Consumer prices rose 3.5% in the year to September, above the Bank's July forecast of 3.0%. The Bank has warned inflation could rise above 4% early next year. Higher energy prices linked to the Iran war are the main driver.

The poll points to a 7-2 vote for a rise. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 to hold rates in September. Governor Andrew Bailey has said the Bank cannot wait for definitive evidence that inflation is becoming embedded.

stories.say: The Trump administration has promised farmers more than fifteen billion dollars in payments, including eight billion to offset high diesel prices, days before the midterms.
stories.stand: The Department of Agriculture announced payments to offset high diesel and fertiliser costs in the final weeks before Tuesday's elections.
body: The US Department of Agriculture has announced more than $15bn in payments and initiatives for farmers in the final weeks before Tuesday's midterm elections. The aid is meant to offset higher diesel and fertiliser costs.

More than half is an $8bn one-time payment for farmers hit by high diesel prices. The department said details would follow this month. Separately, it plans $13.8bn in safety net payments for 2025 corn, soybean, wheat and rice crops.

Diesel averaged $6.32 a gallon on Friday, about 70% higher than a year earlier, according to AAA. Kansas State economist Gregg Ibendahl said the payments would more than cover the rise in fuel costs, but not wider price pressures.
Donald Trump was due to visit Iowa and Kansas on Sunday.

stories.head: NASA's Swift observatory set to fall back to Earth this week
stories.say: NASA's Swift observatory is due to plunge back to Earth this week after twenty-two years in orbit, following a failed attempt by a private spacecraft to boost it higher.
stories.stand: The gamma-ray telescope is expected to re-enter the atmosphere after a failed commercial rescue and the end of its mission.
body: NASA's Swift observatory is expected to re-enter Earth's atmosphere this week, ending a mission of nearly 22 years. The Aerospace Corporation estimated re-entry between 3 and 5 November, WRAL reported.

Swift launched in November 2004 on a planned two-year mission to study gamma-ray bursts. NASA ended science operations on 20 October, after drag from a solar-heated upper atmosphere pulled it down to about 275 km.

A rescue by Katalyst Space Technologies, whose LINK spacecraft was meant to push Swift higher, was called off in August after technical problems. Live Science put the cost of that effort at about $30 million.

Most of the 1.5-ton spacecraft should burn up. Mission scientist Brad Cenko said dense parts such as tungsten pieces and mirror fragments could survive. Any debris would fall between 21 degrees north and south latitude, mostly ocean or desert.

stories.head: NASA's simulated Mars crew emerges after 378 days in isolation
stories.say: Four volunteers have stepped out of NASA's 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston after three hundred and seventy-eight days of isolation, ending the agency's second year-long simulation.
stories.stand: Four volunteers left a 3D-printed habitat in Houston, completing NASA's second year-long Mars analogue mission.
body: The four crew members of NASA's second CHAPEA simulated Mars mission left their habitat at Johnson Space Center in Houston on Saturday after 378 days, Reuters reported.

Ellen Ellis, Ross Elder, Matthew Montgomery and James Spicer entered the 3D-printed habitat of about 1,700 square feet on 19 October 2025. They grew crops, carried out simulated spacewalks and worked with communication delays like those on a real Mars mission.
Johnson Space Center director Vanessa Wyche greeted the crew as they emerged. The crew now faces two weeks of evaluations and debriefings with NASA scientists, Reuters said.

NASA aims to send humans to Mars as early as the 2030s, after returning astronauts to the Moon. It is recruiting for a further year-long analogue mission starting no earlier than August 2027, Engadget reported.

stories.stand: A request for information seeks plans to raise Hubble's orbit, upgrade it or bring it down safely, with a mission needed by 2032.
body: NASA issued a request for information on 29 October asking companies how they could service the Hubble Space Telescope. Options include boosting it higher, enhancing its capabilities or a controlled re-entry.
Hubble has no propulsion to hold its orbit, and NASA's analysis predicts re-entry in 2033 to 2034. The agency says a mission would need to take place by 2032. Responses are due on 30 November.

KeepTrack and Hardware Busters reported that NASA wants a boost to at least 600 km. Hardware Busters said Hubble has sunk to about 470 km and that no funding is currently set aside, while KeepTrack said NASA has not committed to buying a mission.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said Hubble still has important science ahead of it. The request follows the loss of NASA's Swift observatory after a failed commercial attempt to raise its orbit.

stories.head: Voyager 1 back in contact after brief signal loss
stories.say: NASA briefly lost contact with Voyager 1 in October after a group of thrusters went offline, as the probe launched in nineteen seventy-seven nears one light-day from Earth.
stories.stand: NASA says a thruster switch put the 1977 probe into a safe configuration, weeks before it reaches one light-day from Earth.
body: NASA's Deep Space Network could not detect Voyager 1's signal on 18 and 19 October, the agency said on 29 October. The signal returned on 20 October and contact has held since.
Engineers found that one group of thrusters went offline and backups took over. Automatic fault protection then put the spacecraft into a safe configuration. The cause is still being investigated.

In September, engineers swapped three devices on the probe for lower-power alternatives to save energy, NASA said. Without that change, another instrument would probably have been switched off as early as summer 2027.

Voyager 1 launched in 1977 and was about 24 billion km from Earth when the signal was lost. NASA says it will reach one light-day from Earth on 18 November, when radio signals will take 24 hours each way.

stories.head: Sahara meteorite is one of the oldest known rocks from Mars
stories.say: A rose-coloured rock found in the Sahara has been dated to more than four point one billion years old, making it one of the oldest known meteorites from Mars.
stories.stand: Teghaza 001, found in Mali in 2022, formed more than 4.1 billion years ago and records water in the early Martian crust.
body: A Martian meteorite found in the Sahara in 2022 is more than 4.1 billion years old, according to a NASA-funded study in Science. Teghaza 001 is one of the oldest of about 435 known meteorites from Mars.

Researchers dated zircon crystals in the rock. Its chemistry shows it interacted with water as it cooled in the Martian crust, which points to an active early water cycle, NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory said.

Lead author Yang Liu of JPL described the rock as a witness to a time when Mars was likely warmer and wetter, Reuters reported. Co-author Lee Saper said the findings support the idea that early Mars could have harboured life, though the rock does not show whether life existed.
Scientists identified 13 possible source areas in the cratered southern highlands of Mars, NASA said. The rock's exact origin is unknown.

stories.head: Spacewalkers fit seventh new solar array to space station
stories.say: Two astronauts spent more than seven hours outside the International Space Station on Thursday, fitting the seventh of eight new solar arrays meant to boost its power.
stories.stand: Anil Menon and Joshua Kutryk spent more than 7 hours outside the ISS on the 100th US spacewalk.
body: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk installed a new roll-out solar array on the International Space Station on 29 October, NASA said. The spacewalk lasted 7 hours, 11 minutes.

It was the seventh of eight new arrays. NASA says together they should raise the station's generating capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts, including power for a safe, controlled deorbit.

It was US spacewalk 100 and the 285th spacewalk supporting station assembly and maintenance. It was Menon's fourth spacewalk and Kutryk's first. A final spacewalk on 5 November is planned to install the eighth array.

stories.head: Seabirds get jet lag that nudges them off course, study finds
stories.say: Manx shearwaters flying fast across time zones get a kind of jet lag that throws off their sun compass and nudges them slightly off course, Oxford researchers report.
stories.stand: Oxford researchers found fast east-west flights put Manx shearwaters' body clocks out of step with the sun, skewing their sun compass.
body: Manx shearwaters can suffer a form of jet lag on long east-west flights, according to a study published in Science on 29 October. Researchers say the clock mismatch skews their sun compass and pushes them slightly off course.

The University of Oxford team analysed 20 years of GPS tracking data from 1,045 birds on 3,688 foraging trips, its press release said. Birds flying fast eastward could lag local solar time by up to about one hour.

The resulting errors were small. Because the birds keep correcting as they fly, the effect adds only a few kilometres to a homeward trip, the researchers said. Lead author Patrick Lewin told NPR it was a really small addition.

The team said young birds on their first migration, which cannot correct continuously, might miss their destination by much more. Alice Boyle of Western University, who was not involved, praised the study, NPR reported.

stories.head: Ice Age human DNA recovered from Spanish cave dirt
stories.say: Scientists have pulled human DNA from twenty-two-thousand-year-old dirt in a Spanish cave with no bones in it, suggesting western European ancestry survived the last Ice Age.
stories.stand: Researchers extracted human nuclear DNA from a 22,000-year-old layer of El Mirón Cave that holds no human bones or teeth.
body: Researchers have recovered human nuclear DNA from 22,000-year-old sediment in El Mirón Cave in Cantabria, Spain. The layer contains no bones or teeth, the University of Vienna said.

The work is part of a study in Science Advances led by Pere Gelabert and Ron Pinhasi of the University of Vienna. ScienceAlert reported that the DNA came from several individuals, with more males than females.

The El Mirón DNA showed western European ancestry. The researchers say this suggests that ancestry persisted through the coldest phase of the last Ice Age, supporting the Iberian Peninsula as a refuge.

The wider study also found more east-west genetic contact among Gravettian people, active around 34,000 to 25,000 years ago, than earlier data suggested. ScienceAlert noted that modern contamination remains a challenge for the method.

stories.head: Honeybee hives work as layered immune systems, study finds
stories.say: Honeybee hives work like living immune systems, with honey, wax, pollen and propolis combining to fend off harmful microbes, according to Australian researchers.
stories.stand: University of Sydney research on 24 colonies found hive materials combine to repel harmful microbes, with defences shaped by the local landscape.
body: Honeybee hives act like living immune systems that protect colonies from disease, according to a University of Sydney-led study in ISME Communications. Researchers studied 24 colonies across five apiaries in New South Wales.

Materials such as honey, propolis, wax and pollen have antimicrobial and chemical properties that work together, the university said. Defences were tuned more strongly against bacteria than against fungi.

ScienceAlert reported the hives were best protected against Paenibacillus larvae and Paenibacillus alvei, bacteria that can devastate a colony. Stressed colonies were less organised in filtering microbes.

Hive defences varied with the surrounding landscape. Co-author Elizabeth Frost said land clearing and intensive farming could be eroding bees' natural defences, an implication the study did not directly test.

stories.head: May 2024 solar storm breached a radiation barrier around Earth
stories.say: A Japanese satellite found that the huge solar storm of May twenty twenty-four drove high-energy electrons through a radiation barrier around Earth long thought impenetrable.
stories.stand: Data from Japan's Arase satellite show high-energy electrons surged inside a zone of the radiation belts long thought to be shielded.
body: The May 2024 solar superstorm pushed high-energy electrons through a barrier in Earth's radiation belts once thought impenetrable, according to a study in Geophysical Research Letters. The team was led by Yoshizumi Miyoshi of Nagoya University.
Japan's Arase satellite recorded ultra-relativistic electron levels roughly 5,000 times normal inside the barrier, which NASA's Van Allen Probes identified in 2014.
The researchers say the electrons were accelerated locally rather than arriving from outside. The storm depleted cold plasma, letting chorus waves boost electrons to very high energies, they said.
The extra radiation lingered for months, until another storm in October 2024. ScienceAlert noted that the findings rest on one event observed by one satellite.

stories.head: NASA's TRACERS satellites report first results on magnetic reconnection
stories.say: NASA's twin TRACERS satellites suggest that the process letting solar wind energy into Earth's magnetic shield shifts mainly with location rather than over time.
stories.stand: Twin satellites suggest the process that lets solar wind energy into Earth's magnetic shield varies mainly by location, not over time.
body: NASA's twin TRACERS satellites have produced their first scientific results, the agency said on 29 October. A paper in the Journal of Geophysical Research uses data from the mission's first year.

The mission studies magnetic reconnection, where solar wind field lines snap and rejoin with Earth's, releasing energy and flinging particles towards the atmosphere. The paper concludes that reconnection is mainly a spatial process: where it happens shifts, rather than changing over time.
The authors say future measurements will help confirm this. The satellites, launched in 2025, pass through the southern polar cusp several times a day, NASA said.
NASA approved an extension of the prime mission into spring 2027 in September. The principal investigator, David Miles, is based at the University of Iowa.

stories.head: Scientists build a current-driven motor from a single molecule
stories.say: Researchers have built a motor from a single spiral molecule that spins when electric current passes through it, and turns the other way when the voltage is reversed.
stories.stand: A spiral molecule held between gold tips rotates when current flows, with its direction set by voltage polarity, researchers report in Nature.
body: An international team has built a molecular motor from a single screw-shaped molecule, inspired by the Archimedes screw, according to a study in Nature. Electrons passing through the molecule make it rotate.

Reversing the voltage polarity reverses the direction of spin, the researchers said. They report that rotation can raise the molecule's conductance by up to 100 times, a figure that rests largely on simulations.

Oren Tal and Anil Kumar Singh at the Weizmann Institute of Science trapped single molecules between gold tips. Michael Pittelkow's group at the University of Copenhagen made the molecule, and Fabian Pauly's team at the University of Augsburg ran simulations.
The device is a single-molecule laboratory setup. Uses in molecular electronics are described as possibilities rather than demonstrated applications.

stories.head: Congo's Ebola death toll passes 5,000
stories.say: Congo's Ebola outbreak has now killed more than five thousand people, making it the second-deadliest on record, and the strain behind it has no approved vaccine.
stories.stand: The Bundibugyo outbreak declared in May is now the second-deadliest Ebola epidemic on record, with no approved vaccine or treatment.
body: Congo's health ministry says the Ebola outbreak declared in mid-May has killed 5,026 people among 10,351 infected. That is a fatality rate of nearly 50%. About 2,788 people have recovered.

The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, which has no approved vaccine or treatment. It is the second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic that killed about 11,000 people.

The virus has reached 8 of Congo's 26 provinces, with Ituri and North Kivu worst hit. Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria have also reported cases. The Africa CDC says about 80% of new cases come from outside monitored contact chains.
Dr Patrick Otim of the World Health Organization called the toll a tragic milestone. Saudi Arabia suspended travel to and from Kenya on Friday, Al Jazeera reported.

stories.head: Suspected Ebola cases in Nigeria test negative
stories.say: Two people isolated in north-east Nigeria with suspected Ebola have tested negative twice, the country's disease agency says, leaving one confirmed case.
stories.stand: Two people isolated in Yola, Adamawa State, were cleared after two rounds of laboratory tests, Nigeria's disease control agency says.
body: Two people in Yola, Adamawa State, with symptoms suggestive of Ebola have tested negative. The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) announced the results. Their samples went through two rounds of laboratory tests.

The state's emergency operations centre received the report early on 30 October and isolated both people. The NCDC announced the suspected cases on Saturday, stressing that confirmation depended on lab results.

NCDC director-general Dr Jide Idris said there is no laboratory-confirmed case in Adamawa. Nigeria's only confirmed case remains a woman who arrived in Abuja from Uganda and tested positive on 20 October. She was evacuated to Switzerland.
The agency is monitoring 62 contacts linked to her, New Telegraph reports. Six primary contacts were due to leave isolation on Sunday after 21 days without symptoms.

stories.head: US measles cases reach highest yearly total in 35 years
stories.say: America's measles count has reached its highest level in thirty-five years, with Pennsylvania's Lancaster County at the centre of the worst state outbreak.
stories.stand: Federal figures show 4,852 confirmed cases nationally, with Pennsylvania's outbreak centred on Lancaster County the largest of any state.
body: The US has recorded 4,852 confirmed measles cases this year, the highest yearly total in 35 years, according to CDC figures reported by CIDRAP. About 96% of cases were unvaccinated or of unknown vaccination status.
Pennsylvania has the most cases of any state. Lancaster County, home to large Amish and Old Order Mennonite communities, is the epicentre, the Associated Press reports.
Pennsylvania has reported five measles-associated deaths. The CDC acknowledges three measles deaths nationally this year.

CDC data show 92.4% of US kindergarteners had the required MMR shots in 2025-26, down from 95.2% in 2019-20. Outbreaks are considered unlikely at 95% coverage. The AP found some Amish families are now more open to vaccines.

stories.head: Chickenpox jab catch-up starts after 3,037 child hospital stays
stories.say: England has started offering catch-up chickenpox jabs to young children, after health officials reported more than three thousand child hospital admissions last year.
stories.stand: Children in England born between January 2020 and August 2022 are now offered a single MMRV dose under a catch-up programme.
body: A catch-up programme for the chickenpox vaccine began in England on 1 November. It follows UKHSA figures showing 3,037 children and young people under 18 were hospitalised with chickenpox in 2025.
Children born between 1 January 2020 and 31 August 2022 who have not had chickenpox can get one dose of the combined MMRV vaccine. The programme runs until 31 March 2028.
Chickenpox protection joined the routine childhood schedule on 1 January 2026, with doses at 12 and 18 months. Babies under 12 months are not routinely vaccinated.
Babies under one had the highest hospitalisation rate, at 5.8 per 100,000. UKHSA consultant epidemiologist Dr Gavin Dabrera urged parents of eligible children to get them vaccinated.

stories.head: Victoria warns of higher thunderstorm asthma risk
stories.say: Health officials in Victoria warned of a higher risk of thunderstorm asthma on Saturday, as storms moved across areas with heavy grass pollen.
stories.stand: Victoria's chief health officer issued a warning for Gippsland and northern districts as storms met high grass pollen levels.
body: Victoria's Chief Health Officer Caroline McElnay warned of a higher risk of thunderstorm asthma on Saturday. The warning covered all three Gippsland districts and the Northern Country, including Shepparton and Bendigo.
The risk arises when high grass pollen levels meet certain thunderstorms. Strong winds break pollen into small particles that can reach deep into the lungs.
Officials say a wetter winter and spring have produced more grass pollen this year. In November 2016, 10 people died after a thunderstorm asthma event in Melbourne.
People with asthma were advised to carry reliever medication and avoid wind gusts before and during storms, ABC News reported.

stories.head: Child early warning scores to be used in A&E across England
stories.say: A scoring system that flags children whose condition is worsening is to be used in A&E departments across England from this winter, NHS England says.
stories.stand: NHS England says a national paediatric scoring system already used on hospital wards will be rolled out in emergency departments from this winter.
body: A national scoring system for spotting children whose health is deteriorating will be used in A&E departments across England, NHS England says. The rollout starts from this winter.

The National Paediatric Early Warning System scores vital signs such as heart rate, breathing rate, oxygen levels and consciousness. A high score flags a child for more urgent attention. It is already used for inpatients in more than 90 hospitals.
NHS England says those hospitals have seen consistently lower cardiac arrest rates. More than 6 million children attend A&E in England each year.

The system does not replace professional judgement or concerns raised by parents, which can still trigger escalation. The Royal College of Nursing said enough staff, capacity and training would be needed.

stories.head: Alder Hey admits 24 care failures led to toddler's death
stories.say: Alder Hey Children's Hospital has admitted that twenty-four failures in care contributed to a toddler's death after routine skull surgery, and has apologised.
stories.stand: An investigation found the hospital repeatedly miscalculated the girl's early warning score and missed a collapsed lung before she suffered a cardiac arrest.
body: Alder Hey Children's Hospital has accepted responsibility for the death of a toddler and issued a public apology. An investigation found 24 failures in her care that contributed to her death.
She had routine surgery for craniosynostosis, a skull condition, on 29 September 2023. During recovery she developed a collapsed lung.

The investigation found her Paediatric Early Warning System score was repeatedly miscalculated. A correct score would have led to an earlier review and chest X-ray. An abnormal X-ray was not flagged to ward staff, and she suffered a cardiac arrest and an unsurvivable brain injury.
The trust says it has changed its care, and two post-operative procedures are named after her. Her family said her death was preventable.

stories.head: US health insurance enrolment opens with premiums set to rise
stories.say: Sign-ups for Affordable Care Act health plans opened on Sunday, with analysts at KFF expecting average benchmark premiums to rise by thirteen per cent next year.
stories.stand: Affordable Care Act marketplace sign-ups opened on 1 November, with average benchmark premiums expected to rise 13%, according to KFF.
body: Open enrolment for Affordable Care Act marketplace plans began on Sunday 1 November in most US states. It runs until 15 January 2027, and people must sign up by 15 December for coverage from 1 January.
A KFF analysis expects the average benchmark silver plan premium to rise 13%. Rises of 11% are expected in states using healthcare.gov and 16% in states with their own marketplaces.
Many buyers no longer qualify for premium tax credits or cost-sharing reductions. New limits on tax credits for some lawfully present immigrants could leave about 1 million more people uninsured.
About 19.2 million people were actively enrolled in February, according to HHS. KFF's Cynthia Cox said people without subsidies would be hit hardest and expects enrolment to fall.

stories.head: Cuban hospitals short of drugs and power amid US pressure
stories.say: Doctors in Cuba describe running out of cancer drugs and anaesthetics and finishing operations by phone light, as tighter US sanctions squeeze the island's fuel supply.
stories.stand: A 60 Minutes report describes Cuban doctors lacking cancer drugs and operating by phone light as US restrictions tighten.
body: Cuban hospitals face critical shortages of cancer drugs, anaesthetics and laboratory equipment, CBS News's 60 Minutes reported on Sunday. Doctors often turn patients away for lack of supplies.
During power cuts, surgeons have finished operations using phone lights and staff have hand-pumped oxygen to patients, the report said. Many doctors have left the profession or the country.
Cuba lost its main oil supplier after the US captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro on 3 January. Cuban officials say only one oil tanker has reached the island since early January.

Washington says it does not intend to restrict food or medical supplies. But many foreign firms avoid selling to Cuba for fear of US penalties. Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined an interview and issued a statement blaming the Cuban government.

stories.head: Faster walkers had lower death risk in 12-year UK study
stories.say: A study following four thousand older adults in the UK for nearly twelve years found those who walked faster, in tests and daily life, had a lower risk of death.
stories.stand: Research in JAMA Network Open linked both clinic-measured walking speed and everyday pace to lower mortality among older adults.
body: Older adults who walked faster had a lower risk of death over nearly 12 years, according to a study in JAMA Network Open. It followed 4,067 adults in the UK with an average age of about 69. During follow-up, 739 died.
Participants did a short walking test at their usual pace and wore a wrist tracker for 9 days. Healthline reports the data came from the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy.
Each standard increase in clinic walking speed was linked to a 23% lower risk of death after adjustment, Healthline reports. Higher everyday step cadence was linked to a 17% lower risk.
The findings show an association, not proof that walking faster extends life. Participants were generally healthier than the wider group they were drawn from.

stories.head: Daily peanuts linked to better brain insulin response in small trial
stories.say: A small Dutch trial found that eating peanuts daily for sixteen weeks improved older adults' brain response to insulin, though it showed no protection from dementia.
stories.stand: A Maastricht crossover trial of 31 older adults found regional brain changes after 16 weeks, but did not show protection against dementia.
body: Eating 60g of peanuts a day for 16 weeks improved the brain's response to insulin in memory-linked regions. That is the finding of a small trial at Maastricht University Medical Centre. The results were published in Food & Function.
The randomised crossover trial involved 31 healthy adults aged 60 to 75. Changes were seen in areas including the hippocampus, measured by MRI after insulin was given through the nose.
The study did not show that peanuts prevent cognitive decline or dementia, Euronews notes. The sample was small, and larger, longer studies are needed.
The Peanut Institute Foundation funded the study, ScienceDaily reports. The researchers say the funder had no role in design, analysis or writing.

stories.head: Ultrasound-delivered treatment slows brain tumours in mice
stories.say: Scientists in Virginia used focused ultrasound to carry a gene-based treatment past the brain's defences in mice, slowing the growth of glioblastoma tumours.
stories.stand: University of Virginia researchers used focused ultrasound to carry microRNA treatment past the blood-brain barrier in mouse models of glioblastoma.
body: Researchers at the University of Virginia used focused ultrasound to deliver an experimental treatment to brain tumours in mice. The treatment slowed tumour growth and helped the animals live longer, the team reports in the Journal of Clinical Investigation.

The approach uses microRNAs, short genetic molecules that can suppress several cancer-promoting genes at once. Nanoparticles carry them, while MRI-guided ultrasound and microbubbles briefly open the blood-brain barrier.
Glioblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumour in adults and causes more than 13,000 deaths a year in the US. The blood-brain barrier stops many drugs reaching such tumours.
The results come only from laboratory and animal studies. Lead researcher Roger Abounader said the team hopes to move towards clinical trials.

stories.head: Bolivia declares national emergency as El Niño drought spreads
stories.say: Bolivia's President Rodrigo Paz has declared a national emergency over El Niño, as drought spreads across the country and floods loom in the coming rainy season.
stories.stand: A decree frees up resources as drought spreads and officials warn of floods when the rainy season begins.
body: Bolivia's President Rodrigo Paz has declared a nationwide state of emergency over the effects of El Niño. Supreme Decree 5759 was signed on Saturday and published in the official gazette.

Paz said the measure would let authorities send resources more quickly to where they are needed. The decree covers risks from drought, floods, frost, hail, forest fires and overflowing rivers in 2026-2027.

Figures on the drought vary. The Vice Ministry of Civil Defence put affected families at 78,217, while a defence ministry report cited 114,048 families since 1 June, along with 75,013 head of livestock.
Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano warned that some areas face too little rain while others may see floods. The rainy season usually runs from November to March.

stories.head: El Niño brings first floods to Ecuador and Peru
stories.say: Heavy rain linked to El Niño flooded parts of Guayaquil on Sunday, while a storm in the Galápagos left one person dead and more than two thousand affected.
stories.stand: Storms flooded streets in Guayaquil, Tumbes and the Galápagos as the El Niño season's rains intensified at the weekend.
body: Heavy rain linked to El Niño has caused the first floods of the season in Ecuador and Peru, according to the EFE news agency. Guayaquil, Ecuador's most populous city, flooded for the second time in a week on Sunday.
Authorities said at least 83 sectors of the city were flooded and several areas lost power. Some weather stations recorded more than 50 litres per square metre in an hour.
In the Galápagos, rain on Saturday flooded parts of Puerto Ayora, killing one person and affecting more than 2,000 people. Shelters were opened and aid was flown in on military flights.
In Peru, Tumbes airport recorded 21.5mm of rain in one hour on Sunday, El Comercio reported. Health Minister Luis Dyer travelled to Tumbes to coordinate a response, including a field hospital.

stories.head: India braces for Cyclone Murasu as Arnab death toll rises to six
stories.say: A second cyclone in a week, Murasu, is expected to hit Andhra Pradesh overnight into Tuesday, as Odisha's death toll from Cyclone Arnab rose to six.
stories.stand: Forecasters expect Murasu to strengthen before landfall, while Odisha announced relief for families hit by Cyclone Arnab.
body: Cyclone Murasu is forecast to make landfall between Nellore and Narsapur in Andhra Pradesh on the night of 2 to 3 November. The India Meteorological Department expects it to become a very severe cyclonic storm.
Sustained winds of 100-110km/h, gusting to 120km/h, are forecast. Tamil Nadu and Odisha are on alert for heavy rain, and some southern Odisha districts have closed schools until 3 November.
In Odisha, the death toll from Cyclone Arnab rose to six on Sunday, with 10 people still missing. Two bodies were recovered from a hilltop village destroyed by a landslide.
Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi announced relief including 50kg of rice and Rs 2,500 for each flood-hit family in the south. Arnab made landfall in Andhra Pradesh on 28 October.

stories.head: Flash floods force evacuations in Arizona and Colorado
stories.say: Flash flooding forced mandatory evacuations in Sedona, Arizona, on Sunday, while officials in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, warned of potentially catastrophic river flooding.
stories.stand: Pacific storms brought heavy rain to ground already soaked by deadly floods in the US Southwest earlier this autumn.
body: Flash flooding prompted mandatory evacuation orders in parts of the US Southwest on Sunday, the Associated Press reported. In Sedona, Arizona, residents near Oak Creek were told to leave immediately as waters rose.
Sedona Fire District Chief Ed Mezulis said crews were responding to multiple reports of people trapped in their homes. Residents were directed to a local high school.
In Pagosa Springs, Colorado, officials warned of potentially catastrophic flooding. The San Juan River was forecast to crest above 19 feet, higher than the 17.8 feet recorded in the 1911 flood.

The National Weather Service estimated up to 4 inches of rain across the region through Monday. The Weather Channel said the ground was still saturated after a storm the previous week dropped 2 to 5 inches.

stories.head: Delhi turns back 1,539 vehicles on first day of winter pollution curbs
stories.say: Delhi turned back more than fifteen hundred older vehicles at its borders on Sunday, the first day of a winter ban on non-BS-VI vehicles from outside the city.
stories.stand: Officials imposed fines worth Rs 68.4 lakh as limits on older outside vehicles, construction dust and office attendance took effect.
body: Delhi began enforcing its winter pollution rules on Sunday, barring petrol and diesel vehicles from outside the city that do not meet BS-VI emission standards. CNG, electric and essential-service vehicles are exempt.
On the first day, 1,539 vehicles were turned back at border points, according to figures reported by ETV Bharat. Penalties and environmental compensation totalled Rs 68.4 lakh.
Inspectors checked 300 construction sites and found 32 breaching dust rules. Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa urged residents to keep pollution certificates valid.
The entry ban runs until 31 January. Parking fees have doubled and offices must limit physical attendance to 50%, with the rest working from home.
