stories.head: Algal bloom killed more than 8,000 sharks and rays in South Australia
stories.say: More than eight thousand dead sharks and rays were recorded after a toxic algal bloom off South Australia, in what an expert called probably the largest such die-off.
stories.stand: Records compiled by the Great Southern Reef Foundation suggest some rare species with small ranges may face extinction risk.
body: More than 8,200 dead sharks and rays were reported after a toxic algal bloom off South Australia earlier this year, ABC News reported. The records were compiled by the Great Southern Reef Foundation from citizen scientist reports.
They included around 4,500 southern fiddler rays, 850 Port Jackson sharks and 670 wobbegongs. Unreported deaths mean the true toll is likely to be higher.

Professor Charlie Huveneers of Flinders University said it was probably the largest mass mortality ever recorded for sharks and rays. He said recovery would be slow because they mature late and breed rarely.

Rare species with small ranges, such as the pygmy thornback skate, may face extinction risk. The federal environment department said no nominations had been received to list it or the coastal stingaree as threatened.

stories.head: Albany households face costly switch as gas network closes
stories.say: About eight thousand gas customers in Albany, Western Australia, must switch to electricity or bottled gas as the network closes, and local leaders say support falls short.
stories.stand: ATCO will decommission the city's gas network over three years, and the mayor says help for going electric is too small.
body: About 8,000 ATCO customers in Albany, Western Australia, must switch to electricity or bottled gas as the company decommissions its gas network over the next three years, ABC News reported.
The state government's transition package totals $31 million, including $5 million from ATCO. Customers switching to electric appliances can receive up to $2,000.
Albany Mayor Greg Stocks said the package was not big enough to achieve electrification. Energy analyst Ray Wills warned that a cheap bottled gas option could keep households on gas.
Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the government had tried unsuccessfully to keep ATCO in Albany. She said she would prefer residents moved off gas entirely.

stories.head: UN nature talks end with world off track on 2030 goals
stories.say: UN biodiversity talks in Armenia ended on Saturday with all major texts agreed, but countries acknowledged the twenty thirty nature goals will be missed without faster action.
stories.stand: COP17 in Yerevan completed the first global review of nature targets but left key finance decisions to the next summit in Quito.
body: The COP17 UN biodiversity conference in Yerevan, Armenia, ended in the early hours of Saturday, according to Carbon Brief. Countries signed off all major negotiating texts and completed the first global review of the 2030 nature goals.
The review text notes with deep concern that the 2030 targets will not be met without faster action. An accompanying report found the world off track on 22 of 23 targets.
Developed countries missed a goal of raising $20bn a year for nature by 2025. The decision sets up a post-2030 finance mechanism but leaves its form to COP18, to be held in Quito, Ecuador, in 2028.
Russia opposed most references to the High Seas Treaty and to the ICJ climate opinion. COP17 president Hambardzum Matevosyan said countries had achieved more than expected.

stories.head: African negotiators meet in Antalya a week before COP31
stories.say: African climate negotiators opened a two-day strategy meeting in Antalya on Sunday, ahead of the COP31 talks that run from the ninth to the twentieth of November.
stories.stand: The African Group of Negotiators is pressing for adaptation funding as Türkiye prepares to host the UN climate summit.
body: The African Group of Negotiators on Climate Change opened a two-day strategy meeting in Antalya, Türkiye, on Sunday, according to Ghana's MyJoyOnline. It is preparing a common position for the COP31 UN climate talks.
Its chair, Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, stressed unity to strengthen Africa's voice. The group's priorities include adaptation funding and stronger support for climate-vulnerable people.

COP31 runs at the Antalya Expo Centre from 9 to 20 November, The Rio Times reported. A leaders' summit is scheduled for 11 and 12 November, and Türkiye's environment minister said 85 leaders had confirmed.
Preparatory meetings for least-developed countries, small island states and the G77 and China group are due in the days before the talks open.

stories.head: Wind turbines killed 18.7 million bats in the US, study estimates
stories.say: A new study estimates wind farms in the United States killed nearly nineteen million bats between 1981 and 2024, with yearly deaths rising sharply as wind power grew.
stories.stand: Researchers found turbines near rivers and those with lower ground clearance were especially deadly for bats.
body: Wind energy facilities in the US killed an estimated 18.7 million bats from 28 species between 1981 and 2024, according to a study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Euronews reported.
Annual deaths rose from about 100,000 two decades ago to about 1.5 million by 2021. The authors estimated deaths at unmonitored sites statistically, but said data gaps limited their analysis.

Wind farms near rivers had higher fatality rates, and turbines with less ground clearance were especially deadly. A separate European study of 141 wind farms found pausing turbines when bats are most active can cut deaths by more than 80%.

stories.head: Council of Europe report urges planned retreat from eroding coasts
stories.say: A Council of Europe report says coastal erosion already costs European countries over a billion euros a year, and urges moving homes and roads inland from high-risk shores.
stories.stand: The report warns annual losses from coastal erosion could reach €800 billion by 2100 without effective action.
body: A Council of Europe report has urged planned retreat from Europe's most threatened coastlines, Euronews reported on Sunday. It recommends restricting new building on high-risk coasts and moving homes, businesses and infrastructure inland.
The report says erosion already costs 28 European countries more than €1 billion a year. Without effective action, annual losses could reach €800 billion by the end of the century.
More than a quarter of Europe's coastline is eroding, according to figures cited in the coverage. Co-author Anthony Buchanan argued that sea walls are becoming less sustainable as sea levels rise.
Euronews cited Quiberville-sur-Mer in Normandy, where a €9 million project moved a public campsite inland.

stories.head: A year after Typhoon Halong, Alaskan villagers remain displaced
stories.say: A year after the remnants of Typhoon Halong struck south-western Alaska, most residents of the village of Kwigillingok are still living elsewhere, waiting to rebuild.
stories.stand: Only about 30 people have returned to Kwigillingok, which remains under a no-go-home order as funding disputes slow recovery.
body: The remnants of Typhoon Halong hit south-western Alaska on 12 October 2025, Inside Climate News reported. In Kwigillingok, the storm surge lifted 46 of the village's 99 houses off their foundations, and three people died.
A year on, about 30 people have returned to the village, which remains under a no-go-home order. Most of its 361 pre-storm residents are sheltering in Bethel, Anchorage and nearby communities.

Kwigillingok and Kipnuk have voted to relocate to higher ground, but federal and state recovery funding is not designed to move communities. The state has committed $75 million, and its director estimates recovery costs will exceed $400 million.
FEMA denied the state's request for extra permanent housing funding, and the state plans to appeal.

stories.head: FBI blames North Korea for record $6.3bn Binance hack
stories.say: The FBI says North Korean hackers known as TraderTraitor stole more than six billion dollars from Binance, and are now converting the loot into Ethereum to launder it.
stories.stand: The FBI says a North Korean state-backed unit stole the crypto exchange's funds and is preparing to launder them.
body: The FBI said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the theft of $6.3bn in crypto assets from the crypto exchange Binance. It said the attack took place on or about 29 October.

The FBI calls the hackers TraderTraitor, a unit linked to the wider Lazarus Group. It said they were converting the stolen funds into Ethereum and expected further laundering. It also blames the group for a $1.5bn theft from Bybit in 2025.
The blockchain firm TRM Labs had already linked the attack to the unit. It says most of the money left Binance wallets within about 20 minutes. Binance and its partners froze about $3bn.

Binance says an initial investigation pointed to a compromised laptop, with further points of breach found later. Co-CEO Richard Teng called it a complex attack and said the firm would cover customer losses.

body: Binance customers withdrew $3.64bn when the exchange came back online on Sunday, according to Daily Maverick. Binance says that is about 2.1% of its assets and that outflows are stabilising.
Withdrawals are being restored in phases. The first batch covered major tokens including bitcoin, ether, dogecoin and some stablecoins. Binance says other networks will follow after security checks.

The data site DefiLlama showed higher outflows of $4.36bn. Binance says that figure leaves out flows to its new hot wallet.

body: US District Judge Debra M. Brown has denied xAI's request to dismiss a lawsuit brought by the NAACP. The case will now proceed.

The NAACP says xAI ran gas turbines without the required air permits at its data centre operations near Memphis, Tennessee, breaching the Clean Air Act. The suit says at least 35 combustion turbines were installed without permits.
xAI, now owned by SpaceX, argued the turbines were exempt because they were mobile. The judge found the power plant was not a mobile source. She also ruled the plaintiffs had standing.
NAACP director Abre' Connor called the ruling another important victory. SpaceX did not respond to TechCrunch's request for comment.

body: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has proposed 21.3 trillion won for AI and semiconductors in the 2027 budget. He told the National Assembly on Monday that this was nearly double this year's level.

The plan includes 4.7 trillion won for frontier AI development and 2.1 trillion won for power, water and industrial infrastructure. Lee said the government would invest boldly in AI and future growth engines.

body: Juan Atkins, one of the founders of Detroit techno, has died aged 64. His management company, Green Smith Artists, confirmed his death on Instagram on Sunday 1 November.
He had been due to perform at Yu Yu Club in Mexico City on 31 October. Complex reported he was found unresponsive in his hotel room and pronounced dead in hospital. No cause has been given.
Atkins formed the Belleville Three with Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson. He co-founded Cybotron, whose 1983 track Clear sold about 50,000 copies and was sampled by Missy Elliott.
He also founded the Metroplex label and recorded as Model 500. Complex said his 1988 track Techno Music gave the genre its name.

body: The Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza marked the first anniversary of its official opening on Sunday 1 November. It opened in November 2025 after more than 20 years of work, Xinhua reported.

body: Muruwari and Gomeroi filmmaker Allan Clarke has been named artistic director of the Festival du Cinéma Aborigène Australien in Paris, ABC News reported.
The festival is described as the only one in Europe dedicated to Australian First Nations film. Its 11th edition runs from 4 to 6 December at two Paris cinemas.
Founder Greta Morton-Elangué is stepping back from programming for the first time. Clarke, a former ABC journalist who grew up in Bourke, directed The Dark Emu Story and The Bowraville Murders.
Clarke said he wanted to highlight filmmakers challenging the status quo. The programme includes films by Warwick Thornton, Wayne Blair and Danielle MacLean.

stories.head: Australia rest Cummins, Starc and Hazlewood for England white-ball series
stories.say: Australia have rested Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood for their white-ball series against England, with Mitchell Marsh captaining both squads.
stories.stand: Mitchell Marsh will captain both squads for three ODIs and five T20s as Australia's fast-bowling trio prepare for Test cricket.
body: Australia have rested Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood for their white-ball series against England. The fast bowlers will prepare for World Test Championship matches against New Zealand and India.
Mitchell Marsh will captain both squads. The series comprises three one-day internationals and five T20 internationals, starting in Perth on 13 November and ending on 2 December.

Nathan Ellis misses the ODIs with a side strain. Travis Head and Cameron Green are among six players picked for the ODIs but not the T20s. Nikhil Chaudhary, Joel Davies, Lachlan Shaw and Sam Harper are new to the T20 squad.
Selection chair George Bailey said the matches gave players a chance to show their ability against very strong opposition.

stories.head: England knocked out of Rugby League World Cup as Tonga beat Samoa
stories.say: England are out of the Rugby League World Cup after Tonga edged Samoa in Sydney, leaving Australia, New Zealand, Tonga and Samoa to contest the semi-finals.
stories.stand: Tonga's narrow win over Samoa in Sydney ended England's hopes, completing a semi-final line-up without them.
body: England are out of the Rugby League World Cup after Tonga beat Samoa on Sunday. Addin Fonua-Blake scored Tonga's winning try late in the game.
Serious About Rugby League reported a 20-18 score in front of almost 30,000 fans in Sydney. England had needed Tonga to win by a far bigger margin to overtake Samoa on points difference.
Brian McDermott's side had beaten Papua New Guinea 34-12 in their final pool match on Friday. Love Rugby League said it is the first time England have failed to reach the semi-finals.
New Zealand will face Tonga and Australia will play Samoa in the semi-finals.
